solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); the post prints a stub row for the 17ac/12ac 'I TOLD YOU SO' group's 12ac leg mislabelled as 13A (a separate, correctly-answered clue in its own right, YANKS)

clue.text: 'Blue' must out Tony (not working)

indicators.note: something not working is not on, so the little word meaning switched on is taken out of the name
out can mean disordered or wrong, so the remaining letters are put into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, before the deletion

explanation.surface: A call for Tony, now out of a job, to be outed as a purveyor of filth.
explanation.walkthrough: ON is the usual crossword word for working, so 'not working' removes ON from TONY to leave TY, and MUST plus TY is then rearranged into SMUTTY.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue in the sense of rude or obscene, as in a blue joke or film, means much the same as smutty.

clue.text: Tart left in cooler

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so a letter goes into the middle of a word

blocks.note: a fan cools you down
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A tart has been left to set in the fridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A flan is an open pastry case with a filling, the same kind of dish as a tart.

clue.text: Underwear presented to defenders?

definitions.note: describes the thing rather than naming it: the papers handed to defence barristers

blocks.note: first meaning: short close-fitting pants
second meaning: the case papers a solicitor gives to the barrister defending a client

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the legal sense: in Britain a barrister is instructed by receiving a brief from a solicitor.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both close-fitting short pants and the bundles of case instructions handed to barristers in court.

clue.text: see 27dn.
Queasy tum in a dither, Cyclops gets enlightened types

indicators.note: being in a dither is a state of flustered confusion, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: feeling queasy is feeling ill
these three short words rearranged
the setter Cyclops refers to himself, so I

explanation.surface: The setter's stomach is churning nervously while he joins a secretive club of the wise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a' looks like part of the phrase 'in a dither' but is fodder; only 'dither' signals the anagram. A setter naming himself usually gives I or ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Illuminati literally means those who have been lit up, and is used of people claiming special knowledge or wisdom.

clue.text: Sporting a hard-on is function in gender change

indicators.note: a change alters the arrangement, so the word gender is rearranged
one thing in another sits inside it, so the word for function goes inside

blocks.note: to function is to go, as in a machine that goes
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A cheeky claim that arousal is what happens during a gender transition.
explanation.definitionFit: Engorged means swollen with blood, which is the physical state of an erection.

clue.text: Fruity thing at heart, Trump messed with Beryl

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, so only its central letters are kept
something messed with is jumbled up, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: the middle three letters of the surname
taken as written

explanation.surface: Donald Trump, at heart a fruitcake, has been meddling with a woman named Beryl.
explanation.definitionFit: A mulberry is a tree bearing dark juicy berries, so it is a fruit-bearing thing.

clue.text: Hacks need scoop which gives an intrusive view of someone

definitions.text: which gives an intrusive view of someone
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for 'something which gives', a noun

indicators.note: to hack is to chop roughly, so the following words are cut up and reassembled

blocks.note: both words rearranged together

explanation.surface: Tabloid journalists want an exclusive that lets readers pry into a person's private life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hacks' reads as the noun for journalists, the subject of the sentence, but it is the verb signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An endoscope is a medical camera on a tube passed inside the body, literally looking into a person.

clue.text: Gnome's energy on screen died away

indicators.note: something gone away is no longer present, so the letter for died is dropped

blocks.note: go means energy or drive, as in full of go
a window blind screens a room
D is the abbreviation for died, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A gnome's on-screen energy has faded out, like a fading television star.
explanation.definitionFit: Goblins and gnomes are both small grotesque creatures of folklore, close enough to stand in for each other.

clue.text: Wit's drugs trip goes weird

indicators.note: when something goes weird it becomes strange and twisted, so the word is scrambled

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, so more than one is ES
the word rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's clever banter turns strange during an acid trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Esprit is French-derived for lively intelligence and wit, as in esprit de l'escalier.

clue.text: Camp sort of wear?

blocks.note: surface reading: flamboyant, theatrical clothing
setter's reading: camp is where you pitch canvas shelters, so a garment named after a shelter you sleep in

explanation.walkthrough: Camp suggests flamboyant fashion, but the setter means camping: a loose triangular garment named for its shape.
explanation.definitionFit: This loose, wide dress flares from the shoulders like canvas over a pole, hence its campsite-inspired name.

clue.text: see 17ac.
Trump's lot – jerks

blocks.note: first meaning: Americans, informally, the US president's people
second meaning: pulls sharply

explanation.walkthrough: The surface calls Trump's followers idiots, but jerks is the verb for sudden tugs.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for Americans, Trump's countrymen, and also a verb for pulling suddenly and hard.

clue.text: Trapping Brenda, rogue done good – "good for nothing"

indicators.note: to trap something is to hold it inside, so the royal letters are enclosed
a rogue element goes astray, so the word after it is jumbled

blocks.note: done good is slang for done well; the first word is then rearranged
Private Eye calls the late Queen Brenda, and ER is her royal cipher

explanation.surface: A crook who has made good after taking the Queen hostage, now dismissed as worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: In Private Eye the Queen is nicknamed Brenda; ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword shorthand for her.
explanation.definitionFit: A good-for-nothing is an idle useless person, exactly what a ne'er-do-well is.

clue.text: "Strong, stable leader" being deceptive

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of stable is kept

blocks.note: its first letter
trapping someone means catching them out by a trick

explanation.surface: Theresa May's 'strong and stable leadership' slogan is mocked as a con.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong and stable' was Theresa May's 2017 election slogan, which the quotation marks evoke.
explanation.definitionFit: Strapping describes someone big, sturdy and muscular, a near synonym for strong.

clue.text: Hack gets prison (put with drug dealer)

blocks.note: short for penitentiary, an American prison
a pusher sells illegal drugs

explanation.surface: A journalist is jailed and shares a cell with a drug dealer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hack is a drudge writer turning out routine copy, and a pen-pusher is a desk-bound clerical drudge.

clue.text: (& 12ac.) "EU dolt yo-yos wildly after commencement of election" – as we predicted in an earlier edition

definitions.text: as we predicted in an earlier edition

indicators.note: the commencement of a word is where it begins, so its opening letter alone is kept
acting wildly means out of control, so these letters run in a new order
after places the jumbled words behind the single letter rather than before it

blocks.note: its first letter
all the letters of these three words rearranged

explanation.surface: A pro-Brexit idiot flip-flops after an election, as the magazine already forecast.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye spells its own crowing catchphrase this way, punning on the magazine's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The magazine uses this phrase when boasting that a story it ran in a previous issue has come true.

clue.text: Currency holder accepts one definitively loss-making Maxwell publication

indicators.note: something that accepts another takes it in, so the letter goes inside the holder

blocks.note: the single currency of most EU states
a pen holds animals, as in a sheep pen
a means one

explanation.surface: A wallet takes in a pound coin, then a Maxwell newspaper that only lost money.
explanation.walkthrough: The European was a weekly newspaper launched by the tycoon Robert Maxwell in 1990; it never turned a profit and closed in 1998.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Maxwell founded a weekly newspaper under this title, a famously unprofitable venture that eventually folded.

clue.text: Balls is on the up, with attitude – topple!

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top, so the name runs backwards

blocks.note: Ed Balls is a British Labour politician
a pose is an attitude struck, especially for show

explanation.surface: Ed Balls, the Labour politician, is on the rise and full of swagger, urging a coup.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was a Labour Shadow Chancellor; his first name reversed starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To depose a ruler is to remove them from power, which is to topple them.

clue.text: Piss-taking mug drank at ground

indicators.note: something ground up is crushed and broken down, so the letters are remade in another order

blocks.note: both words rearranged together

explanation.surface: A mocking fool got drunk at a football ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Piss is British slang for beer, so a piss-taking mug is one that takes beer, not a mocking fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A tankard is a large drinking mug, traditionally for beer, the thing you take your piss in.

clue.text: Radical publication of bloody Lords member stuffed by papers

indicators.note: something stuffed by another is filled with it, so the abbreviation is placed inside

blocks.note: blood is red
members of the House of Lords are peers
pp is the abbreviation for pages, papers

explanation.surface: A left-wing magazine runs a piece on some wretched peer being smeared by the press.
explanation.walkthrough: Red Pepper is a British left-wing magazine, so the definition is fair; the vegetable is the decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Red Pepper is the title of a British left-wing political magazine, a radical periodical.

clue.text: Fibre fair loosens a fellow inside

indicators.note: loosening something unfastens it, so the letters of the word fall into another order
inside places one piece within another

blocks.note: the word rearranged
taken as written
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A fibre that relaxes a bloke from within, like a gentle diet aid.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffia is a fibre from palm leaves used for weaving baskets and mats.

clue.text: Workers group sex act?

blocks.note: first meaning: a trade organisation of employees
second meaning: a joining in sexual intercourse

explanation.walkthrough: Read together, the words suggest a workers' orgy; split them and there are two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an organised body of employees and a coupling of two bodies in intercourse.

clue.text: C'mon, no screwing, chaplain!?

indicators.note: screwing means twisting round, so the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: all the letters of both words rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone urges a clergyman to stay celibate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no screwing' sounds like a ban on sex, but screwing is the anagram signal. NON-COM here is short for non-combatant.
explanation.definitionFit: An army chaplain does not fight, so is a non-combatant, abbreviated to this informal military shortening.

clue.text: Might Trump, ultimately, have an obligation to Russian leader?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so just the final letter of Trump is kept
a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of Russian is kept

blocks.note: its last letter
to owe is to be under an obligation
its first letter

explanation.surface: Speculation over whether Trump is in hock to Putin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might' looks like the verb opening a question, but it is the noun meaning strength.
explanation.definitionFit: Might as a noun means strength or force, a synonym of power.

clue.text: More bucks for the city

indicators.note: a horse that bucks throws things about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Extra dollars on offer to the City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bucks' looks like dollars and 'the city' like the City of London, but bucks signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Rome is the ancient capital of Italy, often called simply the City or the Eternal City.

clue.text: Screw in Fens, a casual place offering protection

indicators.note: in places the word for screw within the rearranged letters
a casual arrangement is haphazard, so these letters are set down in a loose new order

blocks.note: to have someone is a crude word for having sex with them
the letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: A casual fling in the Fens, the flat marshland of eastern England, offers shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: A refuge where someone is protected from danger or pursuit is called this two-word phrase.

clue.text: (& 4dn.) Stupid, very, to twice opt for May & co

indicators.note: a stupid arrangement is a senseless one, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the little word repeated

explanation.surface: A sneer at those who chose Theresa May's party twice over as remarkably dim.
explanation.walkthrough: Theresa May was the Conservative Prime Minister; Tory is the everyday name for her party.
explanation.definitionFit: Choosing Theresa May and her colleagues at the ballot box means backing the Conservative party.

clue.text: Look into May, dividing social classes, for assurance

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so the word for look sits inside
dividing two things means splitting them apart from within, so this goes between them

blocks.note: A and B are the top grades in the British social classification
Theresa May was Prime Minister, PM
lo is an old word for look

explanation.surface: An inquiry into Theresa May's class divisiveness, in search of confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: British market research grades households from A down to E, so AB means the upper social classes.
explanation.definitionFit: Aplomb is calm self-confidence and composure, the same as assurance.

clue.text: Book old politician with backing of Right-ousting arsehole

indicators.note: ousting something throws it out, so the letter for right is removed
backing means going backwards, so what remains is written in reverse

blocks.note: a Liberal, of the party before the Liberal Democrats
a rotter is a contemptible person
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An old politician publishes a memoir backing a vile figure who ousted the right wing.
explanation.definitionFit: The libretto of an opera or musical is called its book, the text of words sung and spoken.
